subject: Architecture
title: Stonehenge: Engineering Before Writing
description: A quick win: understand Stonehenge: Engineering Before Writing.

hook.text: Stonehenge's largest stones weigh 25 tons each — moved 25 miles without wheels.

buildup.text: Builders dragged the bluestones 150 miles from Wales, possibly on wooden sledges and rollers.

discovery.text: The stones align with the sunrise on the summer solstice, proving deliberate astronomical design.

twist.text: Construction spanned over 1,500 years. No single generation saw it finished.

climax.text: A society with no written language built a monument that encoded the calendar in stone.

punchline.text: They couldn't write a word, but they could build forever.

details.summary: Stonehenge's largest stones weigh 25 tons and were transported 25 kilometers, while its bluestones traveled 250 kilometers from Wales. Built in stages between 3000 and 2000 BCE, the monument demonstrates that preliterate societies could organize complex engineering projects spanning centuries.
details.whyItMatters: Stonehenge proves that monumental engineering predates writing, mathematics notation, and metal tools. Whatever knowledge system its builders used — oral tradition, ritual practice.
takeaways: Largest stones weigh 25 tons, transported 25 km to the site
Bluestones were moved 250 km from quarries in Wales
Built in stages spanning roughly 1,000 years (3000-2000 BCE)

faq.question: How were the stones transported?
faq.answer: The sarsen stones were likely dragged on wooden sledges and rollers from Marlborough Downs, 25 km north. The bluestones may have been transported partly by water on rafts and partly overland from Wales. Recent research suggests glaciers may have moved some bluestones partway.

faq.question: What was Stonehenge used for?
faq.answer: It aligned with summer and winter solstice sunrise and sunset, suggesting astronomical or calendrical purposes. Burial remains indicate funerary functions. It may have served as a healing center, a tribal gathering place, or a sacred site.
